summary_html: CPS **screens out** a report (no investigation) or closes as **unfounded** after minimal review. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on operating screening criteria and recordkeeping; federal reviews (CFSR) assess decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening & intake system requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review of state screening and responses

key_cases.case_name: Hennepin County Community Services Department v. Hale
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the Commissioner of Administration's order requiring the county to correct a social-services report, holding substantial evidence supported the conclusion that the report was inaccurate in finding the abuse allegation substantiated.
key_cases.relevance: It shows the remedy when an agency records a substantiated conclusion the record does not support.
key_cases.quote: there is substantial evidence in the record to support the Commissioner's decision that the contested report was inaccurate in concluding that the report of abuse by Johnston was substantiated

key_cases.holding: Reversing the court of appeals and reinstating a wrongful-death complaint, the court held that a common-law negligence action may be maintained against a county and its child-protection workers for negligence in the investigation of, and intervention in, reports of suspected child abuse required under the Child Abuse Reporting Act.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling Minnesota authority that closing a report as unfounded is not immune from review: the county here sent the father a letter saying no abuse had occurred, and the child was beaten to death eleven days later.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, we hold that a cause of action can be maintained for negligence in the investigation of child abuse and neglect reports as required under CARA.

key_cases.holding: Affirming summary judgment, the court held that the Child Abuse Reporting Act imposes no duty between a mandated reporter and the abused child that can support a negligence action, so failure to report gives rise to no civil cause of action.
key_cases.relevance: It is the foundation of the no-civil-remedy rule, which Radke later confined to failures to REPORT as distinct from negligence in the county's own investigation.
key_cases.quote: Since CARA created the duty to report, a civil action cannot lie outside the express or clearly implied language of the statute.

state_agency.name: Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families
state_agency.hotline: No statewide hotline. Call the county or Tribal child protection agency where the child lives — the directory link is on dcyf.mn.gov/individuals-and-families/report-abuse

timeline_requirements.deadline: Safety assessment completed at the face-to-face contact with the child and the child's primary caregiver, which must be sufficient to ensure the immediate safety of the child
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of a screened in report
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Minn. Stat. § 260E.20; subd. 2(a) requires the face-to-face contact to be sufficient to complete a safety assessment and ensure the immediate safety of the child.

Not specified by statute; Minn. Stat. § 260E.24, subd. 3 requires the two determinations at the conclusion of the investigation and subd. 5 requires written notice within ten working days of that conclusion.

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of notice of the investigating agency's final determination regarding maltreatment
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Minn. Stat. § 260E.33; subd. 2 requires the written request within 15 calendar days after receipt of notice of the final determination, subd. 3 allows a fair hearing only after the agency denies the reconsideration request or fails to act on it within 15 working days, and subd. 1 provides no reconsideration after a family assessment or noncaregiver human trafficking assessment because no maltreatment determination is made.
